title: The prostration of thanks
hookLine: a single prostration at good news (Abu Dawud)

cards: Ka'b ibn Malik has been waiting a long time. He stayed home from a military expedition with no excuse, and when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ returned, Ka'b told the plain truth instead of inventing one.

Since then, by his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari, people have stopped speaking to him. Then one morning, after the dawn prayer, on the roof of his house, he hears a voice shouting from a hill: Ka'b ibn Malik, good news!
Before he stands, before he runs to anyone, before he says a word, his body answers. He falls down in prostration.

teach.b: Sujud al-shukr means the prostration of thanks: a single prostration, on its own, outside the regular prayer, made when good news arrives or a harm is lifted. First, the Prophet's habit.
Abu Dawud records that when something delighted him, or he was given good news, he would fall down in prostration, giving thanks to God. No bowing first, no units, no closing salam. Just down.
Second, why the body. In the five prayers the prostration is the lowest point, forehead on the floor.
Using that posture for joy says the place of greatest humility is also the place of thanks. Third, the promise behind it.
Pickthall's translation of surah fourteen has God say: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more." Thanks, in that verse, isn't just good manners. It opens a door.
Fourth, the details, where scholars differ.
Some hold that because it's a prostration, it needs wudu and facing the qibla, like prayer. Others say it isn't a prayer at all, so good news can be answered on the spot.
Within the Maliki school a well-known view did not encourage it, while others in the same school accepted it. Go back to Ka'b on his roof.

teach.h: IF YE GIVE THANKS, I WILL GIVE YOU MORE.
teach.b: The report doesn't have him checking his wudu or which way he faced. It just says he fell down. Whatever a school decides about the details, the first move is the same.
Good news comes, and the forehead goes to the ground.

how: On hearing good news or being spared a harm, Muslims who keep this practice make a single prostration of thanks, outside the regular prayer; schools differ on whether wudu and facing the qibla are needed for it.

o: the two prostrations that mend a slip in prayer
a full prayer of thanks with bowing and units

games.q: you're Ka'b. you've waited a long time, cut off for telling the truth. a voice shouts from the hill: good news! what do you do first?
o: run to the Prophet to hear it for yourself.
fall down in prostration where you are.
wait to be sure it's true.
games.why: he fell down in prostration on the spot, then went to the Prophet (Sahih al-Bukhari).

practice: Let one piece of good news from the last while come back in full: a test result, a message, a child's laugh, a debt paid off, a pain that eased.

If you pray, you can make a single prostration of thanks now, or keep the habit ready for the next good news. If you don't, bow your head or rest your palms flat on the floor, and let the body say thanks before the mouth does.

wordCard.voice: Sujud al-shukr. The prostration of thanks: one prostration, on its own, when good news comes. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the prostration of thanks. shukr is gratitude.

carryVoice: Your line: down, in thanks. The lowest place is also the place of joy. Until tomorrow.
